question: Can automatically generated semantic part/path annotations, supervised fine-tuning on arbitrary partial canvases, and multi-turn GRPO with per-step rendered-state rewards train one VLM agent to generate detailed vector sketches part by part, outperform sequential and one-shot baselines in-domain, and support localized editing?

key_findings.claim: Author-reported data contribution: ControlSketch-Part adds two-to-five semantic parts, exhaustive path-to-part assignments, and a global caption to 35,000 synthetic professional-style sketches across 15 categories through a seven-stage VLM proposal-critique-revision pipeline.
key_findings.evidence: Gemini 3.0 Pro proposes parts from a raster rendering, critiques and revises them, assigns every raw SVG path to exactly one part, critiques the assignment using an original rendering plus a color-coded diagnostic panel, revises it, and derives the caption from refined parts. Appendix B gives the actual prompts and JSON-schema constraints, including exhaustive/non-overlapping descriptions, every path used exactly once, and every part receiving a path. No manual annotation-accuracy estimate, inter-rater check, held-out pipeline audit, or comparison of proposal-only versus critique/revision quality is reported.

anchors.section: Figure 2 and 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
3 Automated Part Annotation / 3.1 Data Collection Pipeline
Completion of 3.1 and 3.2 Our Dataset: ControlSketch-Part

key_findings.claim: Author-reported SFT mechanism: arbitrary part-order permutations turn each sketch into many one-step continuation examples, teaching valid cubic Bézier output from oracle partial canvases but not yet exposing the model to its own errors.
key_findings.evidence: For each sketch the authors sample at most 20 permutations of its parts. Each training example supplies the global caption, next-part description, prior descriptions/paths, remaining-part count, and rasterized current canvas; the target is only the next part's paths. Outputs are newline-separated M/C cubic Bézier commands with eight coordinates. This gives order flexibility and format grounding, while the paper explicitly identifies the oracle-state versus self-generated-state gap that motivates RL.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported RL mechanism: multi-turn process-reward GRPO normalizes rewards separately at each sketching step, using the current-step standardized reward as the advantage rather than one group-wide or terminal signal.
key_findings.evidence: All G rollouts for a prompt have the same number of parts T. For each t, rewards across trajectories form R_t; Eq. 5 standardizes within R_t and Eq. 6 sets A_t directly to that standardized immediate reward. The visual reward is DreamSim cosine similarity between generated and ground-truth partial renderings; a final path-count reward max(0,1-|N_gt-N|/N_gt) is added with λ=1. Invalid formatting receives the group minimum and terminates the rollout. Appendix Algorithm 1 confirms full multi-turn trajectories are sampled before token-level GRPO updates.

anchors.section: Process-reward calculation, DreamSim reward, path-count reward

key_findings.claim: Author-reported training recipe: a Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B agent is LoRA-tuned first on cheaper Gemini-annotated SFT data and then on ControlSketch-Part RL data, with several choices that materially define the result.
key_findings.evidence: Rank-64 LoRA SFT uses learning rate 2e-4, batch 128, and 5,400 steps; RL uses 1,000 additional steps, batch 8, group size 8, learning rate 3e-6, λ=1, and no KL penalty. Adam uses β1=.9, β2=.95. SFT coordinates are rounded to tens whereas RL keeps integers. The SFT set is annotated by Gemini 2.5 Flash and ControlSketch-Part by Gemini 3.0 Pro, but exact split sizes, category balance, prompt counts, seeds, sampling temperatures, and train/validation/test separation are absent.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported automatic evaluation: the full SFT+RL agent attains Long-CLIP 0.307, close to the paper's ground-truth reference 0.312 and above SFT-only 0.300 and all three deployed baselines.
key_findings.evidence: PDF Figure 5 reports GT 0.312, Ours SFT+RL 0.307, Ours SFT 0.300, SketchAgent 0.288, Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.285, SDXL+SwiftSketch 0.281, and random curves 0.188. The metric compares the final rasterized sketch with concatenated part descriptions. The paper appropriately uses Long-CLIP rather than its DreamSim training reward, but calls GT an upper bound without a theorem and reports neither number of test sketches, dispersion, repeated decoding, confidence intervals, nor significance.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported user study: participants prefer the full agent over each tested baseline, with the largest margin over the two-stage SDXL+SwiftSketch system.
key_findings.evidence: The Prolific study collects 426 responses per step-quality comparison from 142 participants and 560 per final-quality comparison from 146, totaling 3,092. PDF Figure 6 reports step preference for Ours SFT+RL of 83.1% versus SFT-only and 70.0% versus SketchAgent; final-quality preference is 84.1% versus SFT-only, 77.5% versus SketchAgent, 66.1% versus Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 91.1% versus SDXL+SwiftSketch. The manuscript does not report prompt sampling, assignment design, exclusions, demographics, tie handling, participant dependence, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported controlled ablation supports both multi-turn rollouts and per-step rewards, but only on a different 3B backbone and one unreplicated metric.
key_findings.evidence: On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Table 1 gives Long-CLIP 0.281 for single-turn terminal-reward RL, 0.286 for multi-turn outcome-reward RL, and 0.298 for multi-turn process-reward RL. Thus multi-turn adds 0.005 and step reward adds another 0.012 in this setup. The paper gives no seeds, variance, training-budget parity details, SFT-only row for this 3B experiment, or confirmation that the same increments hold for the final 30B-A3B model.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported editability is demonstrated qualitatively rather than evaluated as an editing task.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 shows stroke removal and replacement, and Figure 9 shows two branches from different initial canvases plus a change from long hair to short hair whose later part descriptions remain fixed. These examples support localized continuation and some spatial conditioning, but there is no edit-success metric, unchanged-region preservation score, instruction-following benchmark, user study specifically for editing, or comparison with SketchAgent's conversational modification capability.

key_findings.claim: Author-stated failure audit: the path-count reward can stop a part before it is complete, rare semantic topology can be drawn incorrectly, and RL does not eliminate spatial misalignment.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix E.1 attributes a missing car wheel to reaching the ground-truth path count, shows failure on a rare vertically oriented oval rear wheel, and shows a jacket displaced far right from the legs. These are direct counterexamples to complete part realization, compositional topology, and perfect localized placement within the in-domain workflow.

anchors.section: Appendix E.1 Failure cases / Figure A16

key_findings.claim: Author-stated OOD limitation: most unseen object categories collapse, semantically nearby inputs are replaced by trained-category analogues, and unrelated requested parts usually fail to attach correctly.
key_findings.evidence: For unseen bed, fork, whale, and helicopter, the appendix says meaningful sketches usually fail. Tiger, camel, shark, bus, and spider instead resemble trained bear, horse, fish, car, and crab categories. Elephant, octopus, and submarine are occasional better cases when descriptions are generic. Adding crab pincers to an angel, walking legs to a fish, or feathered wings to a chair mostly fails. This shows strong closed-category bias despite free-text conditioning.

key_findings.claim: Author-stated coordinate limitation: numerical prediction and sampling sometimes create drastically misplaced strokes even in-distribution; the worst-output gallery makes this failure concrete but gives no frequency estimate.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix E.2 attributes failures to imprecise coordinate prediction compounded by temperature sampling and calls the displayed cases infrequent edge cases. PDF Figures A19 across pages 48-50 show fragmented or displaced hair/body/clothing, malformed vehicles, disconnected animal parts, and paths extending far from intended structures. The appendix supplies neither an incidence rate nor a selection protocol for 'lowest-quality' outputs.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer novelty audit: the paper's strongest support is for an in-domain combination of semantic part data and self-generated-canvas RL, not for general vector-graphics generation, generic annotation, or universal editability.
key_findings.evidence: The main quantitative test stays within ControlSketch's 15 categories; no annotation-quality score or OOD quantitative result is given, and the appendix reports broad OOD failure. SketchAgent already supplies training-free sequential conversational vector sketching; Reason-SVG already combines SFT and GRPO; rendering-aware RL already uses rendered visual feedback; and the earlier VectorGym already combines expert SVG sketch/edit data, a Qwen3-VL policy, GRPO, and rendering rewards. StarVector and OmniSVG use far larger multimodal SVG corpora, while the later RefineSVG supplies a current render-observe-correct competitor. What remains distinctive is semantic path-level part annotation plus per-turn group-normalized partial-render rewards in one trained sketch agent.

anchors.section: 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models

method.core_idea: Turn a synthetic vector-sketch corpus into semantic, path-addressable multi-turn trajectories; teach next-part generation from oracle partial canvases with SFT; then close the exposure gap by rolling the agent through its own canvases and applying group-relative, per-step visual rewards.
method.mechanism: A seven-call Gemini 3.0 Pro annotation pipeline proposes/critiques/revises two-to-five parts, assigns every SVG path, critiques the color-coded assignment, revises it, and writes a caption. The Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B policy receives the current raster, overall caption, requested next-part text, prior part descriptions and SVG paths, and remaining turn count, and emits newline-separated cubic Bézier paths. SFT expands each sketch through up to 20 part permutations using ground-truth partial states. RL samples eight complete trajectories, renders each partial canvas with CairoSVG, compares it with the matching ground-truth partial rendering in DreamSim space, adds a final path-count term, standardizes reward across rollouts independently at each turn, and performs clipped token-level GRPO; malformed outputs receive minimum reward and terminate.
assumptions: Gemini-generated decompositions and path assignments are accurate enough to serve as ground truth without a measured human audit.
Two to five parts capture the meaningful structure of every sketch in the selected corpus.
The synthetic SDXL/SDS-derived ControlSketch distribution is representative of useful human vector-sketch workflows.
Random part permutations produce physically plausible drawing orders and teach order-invariant continuation.
The global caption, requested part, previous text/paths, and raster together fit the context and disambiguate the next action.
A restricted M/C cubic Bézier vocabulary with shared style attributes is expressive enough for the claimed sketch domain.
DreamSim similarity to the matching ground-truth partial sketch aligns with semantic correctness and aesthetic quality of a creative alternative.
Rewards standardized within each turn have sufficient variance; Eq. 5 gives no explicit zero-standard-deviation safeguard.
Using only the immediate standardized step reward as A_t provides adequate credit for actions whose effects persist into later canvases.
Matching the exact final ground-truth path count is beneficial even though equally good sketches may need different numbers of strokes.
Turning off the KL penalty does not cause harmful drift during the 1,000 RL steps.
Long-CLIP on concatenated part descriptions measures final instruction faithfulness despite its compressed score range.
The in-domain trained 30B-A3B agent can be fairly compared with zero-shot proprietary VLMs and a text-to-image-plus-vectorization pipeline.
Crowd forced choice without reported uncertainty is stable enough to support the claimed preference ordering.
A small number of qualitative edit branches demonstrates general localized editability.

techniques.role: Uses repeated VLM roles to improve semantic part labels before they become training targets.
Renders assigned paths and part descriptions in matched colors so a VLM can detect path-to-part mistakes.
Requires every SVG path to map to exactly one nonempty semantic part.
Creates arbitrary-order next-part examples from each labeled sketch.
Feeds each newly rendered partial canvas back to the multimodal policy at the next turn.
Restricts output to newline-separated move/cubic-curve commands and coordinates.
Computes GRPO baselines separately for each part index across same-length rollouts.
Supplies dense visual feedback by comparing every cumulative generated canvas with its matching ground-truth partial canvas.
Discourages reward-driven stroke proliferation by rewarding proximity to the reference path count.
Assigns minimum reward and stops a rollout when SVG action syntax is invalid.
Allows users to remove existing strokes or change one part description and regenerate from that intermediate canvas.

limitations: Author-stated: ControlSketch covers only 15 object categories, and data coverage is the main bottleneck to a general sketching agent.
Author-stated: most unseen categories do not yield meaningful sketches; semantically nearby OOD inputs often collapse to trained bear, horse, fish, car, or crab classes.
Author-stated: the agent usually cannot attach unrelated out-of-domain parts accurately.
Author-stated: the fixed-path-count reward can cause premature stopping and incomplete parts.
Author-stated: rare semantic topologies and residual part misalignment remain failure modes after RL.
Author-stated: coordinate prediction and temperature sampling can create drastically degraded stroke placement even in-distribution.
Author-stated: generation is serial, one part at a time; planning, parallel part agents, self-evaluation, and selective regeneration are future work.
Reviewer-identified: the automatic labels are treated as ground truth without measured semantic-part or path-assignment accuracy.
Reviewer-identified: 'generic' annotation is demonstrated with one VLM family on one synthetic sketch corpus and is not tested on another SVG dataset or style.
Reviewer-identified: exact SFT/RL/test split sizes and leakage controls are absent, despite ControlSketch-Part being both the core data source and evaluation domain.
Reviewer-identified: the final 30B-A3B model is compared against zero-shot services and a cascaded image baseline rather than a matched trained backbone/data baseline.
Reviewer-identified: cited direct RL competitors Reason-SVG and Rendering-Aware RL are not implemented as experimental baselines.

Reviewer-identified: VectorGym was submitted before this paper and is an especially close omitted comparator: it provides expert-authored SVG sketch/edit benchmarks and trains Qwen3-VL with curriculum GRPO and rendering-based rewards, yet no matched evaluation or priority discussion is given.
Reviewer-identified: Long-CLIP has a compressed 0.281-0.307 non-random range and no uncertainty, so rank stability is unknown.
Reviewer-identified: the user study lacks confidence intervals, participant-level analysis, prompt-selection details, and statistical testing.
Reviewer-identified: editability and controllability are supported by selected examples, not a benchmark or causal localization metric.
Reviewer-identified: the reward prefers reproduction of one synthetic reference rather than valid creative alternatives, potentially penalizing diversity.
Reviewer-identified: Eq. 5 gives no stated handling for zero within-turn reward variance, and Eq. 6 gives earlier actions no explicit credit from later improvements or failures.
Reviewer-identified: a path-count target derived from the reference is not invariant to equally good stroke decompositions and directly causes documented omissions.
Reviewer-identified: only M/C cubic Bézier curves with shared styling are generated, excluding broader SVG structure, color, fills, text, grouping, and transformations.
Reviewer-identified: no inference latency, training FLOPs, annotation cost, memory usage, or end-to-end reproducibility package is reported.
Reviewer-identified: proprietary Gemini/Claude versions and the hosted Tinker training service make exact long-term reproduction vulnerable to service drift.
Reviewer-identified: pages 48-50 show severe worst-case failures but the claim that they are very infrequent has no measured prevalence.
failure_modes: The agent reaches the reference stroke count before completing the requested part and stops with missing geometry, as in the omitted wheel.
Rare spatial/topological phrases such as a vertically oriented rear wheel are rendered as familiar but incorrect structures.
A semantically correct part is placed away from the existing body, leaving unnatural gaps or overlaps.
Early coordinate errors persist in every later raster observation and compound through the multi-turn canvas.
For unseen categories the policy emits incoherent strokes rather than composing known parts into a new object.
OOD prompts collapse to nearest training categories, for example tiger to bear or bus to car.
Cross-category requested parts are ignored, malformed, or assimilated into the familiar host object's geometry.
Temperature sampling yields strokes far outside the intended component even for an in-domain category.
DreamSim can reward raster similarity while semantic part identity, vector topology, edit structure, or path economy is wrong.
The reference path-count term penalizes alternative but efficient decompositions and encourages dataset-specific stroke statistics.
When all rollouts at a step receive the same reward, unstabilized standardization can be undefined or numerically unstable.
Immediate-only process advantages can optimize a locally plausible part that blocks better geometry at later turns.
Critique/revision annotations can consistently propagate VLM misconceptions because no human adjudication catches shared errors.
A baseline requiring long compositional text can be disadvantaged by its input interface rather than its vector-generation ability.
A user can remove strokes that also carry structure for multiple semantic concepts because the path partition is forced to be exclusive.
The compact curve language cannot express filled, colored, hierarchical, or mixed-primitive SVG designs targeted by broader vector generators.
reusable_insights: Represent an evolving visual artifact in both symbolic form and rendered form; each catches errors the other hides.
Use proposal-critique-revision with schema checks for scalable labels, but audit a statistically meaningful sample with humans before calling them ground truth.
Color-coded diagnostic renderings are a simple transferable interface for checking assignments between text labels and vector elements.
Permutation augmentation can teach continuation from arbitrary intermediate states and enable branching workflows without collecting each order manually.
Separate format learning from self-generated-state training: SFT establishes a valid action language, and on-policy rollouts address exposure bias.
For fixed-length structured trajectories, compute group-relative reward baselines at homologous steps so easy and hard stages do not distort one another.
Render discrete programs and reward their perceptual consequences when differentiable rendering is unavailable.
Pair perceptual rewards with structural constraints, but avoid reference-specific proxies such as exact action counts when multiple solutions are valid.
Evaluate the process and the final artifact separately; a plausible endpoint can hide a poor or uncontrollable trajectory.
Publish worst cases and OOD nearest-class substitutions because average embedding similarity can conceal category memorization.
A convincing editing claim needs both target-region success and preservation of untouched regions.
Baseline comparisons should distinguish task-specific training gains from architectural or interaction gains by matching data, backbone, and compute.
open_questions: What are human-verified precision and recall for part decompositions and path assignments before and after each critique/revision stage?
How much does each of the seven annotation stages improve downstream generation, and is the expensive Gemini 3.0 Pro pass necessary?
What are the exact dataset splits, and are near-duplicate ControlSketch source images or captions separated across SFT, RL, validation, and test?
Does process-reward GRPO still help the 30B-A3B model across seeds, or is the reported 3B ablation backbone-specific?
Would return-to-go over future process rewards outperform the immediate Eq. 6 advantage for parts whose quality matters later?
How should group normalization handle zero reward variance at a turn?
Can a learned complexity prior replace exact reference path count and eliminate premature stopping without stroke explosion?
How do results change under a matched Qwen backbone trained with outcome reward, RLRF-style final rendering reward, or Reason-SVG hybrid reward?
Does the method outperform SketchAgent on conversational correction, undo, and multi-round refinement rather than only predefined next-part prompts?
Can localized editing be scored with target-part fidelity, non-target preservation, topology, and human effort?
How rapidly does quality decay with number of parts/turns, and can self-critique or selective regeneration arrest the accumulation?
Can scaling beyond 15 synthetic categories prevent nearest-class substitution, and how much real human sketch data is required?
Would continuous coordinate heads, constrained geometry, or tool-based snapping reduce the severe numerical-coordinate failures on pages 48-50?
Can the semantic part/path representation extend to color, fill, layers, groups, and mixed SVG primitives while retaining editability?
What are end-to-end annotation/training/inference costs and latency relative to training-free SketchAgent and full-SVG VLMs?

competitive_landscape.title: SketchAgent: Language-Driven Sequential Sketch Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: SketchAgent already performs sequential vector sketch creation, modification, and refinement with an off-the-shelf multimodal LLM and an in-context action language, requiring no training. The target trains an open-weight Qwen policy on path-level semantic parts and partial canvases and adds per-step RL, producing more detailed in-domain sketches but losing SketchAgent's demonstrated open-ended conversational breadth and relying on a narrow corpus.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:2411.17673v1; submitted 2024-11-26; no revision as of 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: VectorGym: A Multitask Benchmark for SVG Code Generation, Sketching, and Editing
competitive_landscape.difference: VectorGym predates the target's submission and already supplies expert human-authored Sketch2SVG and complex multi-step SVG editing data, plus text generation and captioning, and trains a Qwen3-VL 8B model with curriculum GRPO and rendering-based rewards. It is therefore a strong priority and matched-method threat absent from the paper. The target remains distinct in semantic path-to-part partitions, arbitrary part order, cumulative partial-canvas text conditioning, and a reward normalized at homologous part steps rather than broad multitask SVG code training.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:2603.29852v1; submitted 2026-02-22; no revision as of 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Reason-SVG: Enhancing Structured Reasoning for Vector Graphics Generation with Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Reason-SVG also uses SFT followed by GRPO for vector graphics, but generates explicit Drawing-with-Thought rationales and full SVGs under hybrid structural, semantic, reasoning, and visual rewards using SVGX-DwT-10k. The target's narrower innovation is multi-turn partial-canvas observation and homologous step rewards tied to semantic sketch parts; it omits a direct experimental comparison.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:2505.24499v2; submitted 2025-05-30; revised 2026-04-09; live v2 title checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Rendering-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Vector Graphics Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: RLRF renders complete autoregressive SVG rollouts for image-to-SVG vectorization and compares them with the raster input, improving fidelity and efficiency over SFT. Both works obtain RL signal through a non-differentiable renderer; the target adds text-conditioned part trajectories and intermediate reference canvases, whereas RLRF covers broader SVG code and does not require a semantic part partition.

competitive_landscape.title: SwiftSketch: A Diffusion Model for Image-to-Vector Sketch Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: SwiftSketch learns subsecond image-conditioned generation by jointly denoising stroke control points, and its ControlSketch synthesis process supplies the 35,000 sketches annotated by the target. It generates whole sketches without free-text semantic parts; the target adds an upstream text-to-image dependency when using SwiftSketch as a baseline and focuses on interactive generation rather than SwiftSketch's speed and open-image conditioning.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:2502.08642v1; submitted 2025-02-12; no revision as of 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: StrokeFusion: Vector Sketch Generation via Joint Stroke-UDF Encoding and Latent Sequence Diffusion
competitive_landscape.difference: StrokeFusion jointly encodes normalized stroke sequences and unsigned-distance-field maps, then diffuses stroke-level latent position, scale, and trajectory on QuickDraw and supports interpolation. It offers a holistic vector representation and class-domain evaluation, while the target uses a language/VLM action policy and semantic parts for progressive control; neither demonstrates broad OOD generalization.

competitive_landscape.title: DiffSketcher: Text Guided Vector Sketch Synthesis through Latent Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: DiffSketcher optimizes a set of Bézier curves jointly at test time under diffusion SDS and attention-based initialization, giving flexible text-driven whole-sketch synthesis without training a sketch policy. The target is faster at learned inference and exposes semantic stages/edit points, but is category-bound and does not compare quality, diversity, or compute with the current revised DiffSketcher record.

competitive_landscape.title: StarVector: Generating Scalable Vector Graphics Code from Images and Text
competitive_landscape.difference: StarVector trains a multimodal language model on SVG-Stack's two million samples and evaluates image-to-SVG, text-to-SVG, and diagram generation with broad primitives and compactness-aware analysis. The target handles a narrower monochrome cubic-curve sketch language but adds explicit part-by-part interaction and intermediate visual feedback; its 35,000-sample scope and benchmark are much smaller.

competitive_landscape.title: OmniSVG: A Unified Scalable Vector Graphics Generation Model
competitive_landscape.difference: OmniSVG discretizes SVG commands/coordinates and trains a unified VLM on the two-million-sample MMSVG-2M corpus for multimodal conditional SVG generation under a standardized evaluation protocol. It generates richer full SVG structures but not semantic part trajectories; the target's contribution is the interactive process representation, while OmniSVG is a stronger scale and vector-language comparator absent from experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: RefineSVG: Visual Feedback-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Image-to-SVG Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: RefineSVG postdates the target but is current by the review cutoff. It renders an initial full SVG, feeds a visual residual map back for one correction step, compresses SVG tokens with a semantic vocabulary, and trains through SFT, rejection sampling, and agentic RL. Unlike the target it is image-conditioned, broader in SVG structure, and not semantic-part sequential; unlike RefineSVG, the target supplies multiple human-interpretable part turns and intermediate ground-truth partial rewards rather than a single corrective loop.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:2607.27699v1; submitted 2026-07-30; no revision as of 2026-08-23; ACM MM 2026 accepted

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a generic scalable semantic part-annotation pipeline, a new ControlSketch-Part dataset and multi-turn benchmark, and a novel process-reward GRPO algorithm that enables one VLM to generate detailed vector sketches part by part with text control and localized editing.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper provides seven explicit annotation prompts, a 35,000-sketch in-domain corpus, a Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B SFT+RL agent, exact Long-CLIP and forced-choice improvements over four deployed variants/systems, a 3B RL ablation, extensive qualitative sequences, and candid failure/OOD appendices.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The credible novelty is the specific combination of VLM-generated semantic path partitions, arbitrary-order partial-canvas SFT, and turn-matched group-relative DreamSim rewards for a trained vector-sketch agent. Sequential language-driven sketching predates it in SketchAgent; SFT+GRPO vector generation predates it in Reason-SVG; rendering-feedback RL predates it in RLRF; and, most importantly, the earlier VectorGym already combines expert SVG sketch/edit data, Qwen3-VL GRPO, and rendering rewards. Large VLM SVG datasets/generators predate it in StarVector and OmniSVG, while RefineSVG is a later current closed-loop rendering-feedback competitor. The in-domain gains are substantive but do not validate generic annotation, broad OOD text-to-vector generation, quantitative editability, or superiority under matched data/backbone/compute. Appendix failures narrow the result to the 15-category ControlSketch distribution and familiar part compositions.

reviewer_notes: Secondary verification independently re-read all 50 physical pages of the exact current arXiv:2603.19500v2 PDF, including the complete main paper, 42 references, Algorithm 1, every data-collection prompt, all additional result and dataset galleries, Appendix E failures/OOD discussion, and pages 48-50 worst outputs; arXiv's versioned PDF was byte-identical to the indexed cache at SHA-256 d3544279e5bc3c4b80681ee87ee4cc91c54cf382bec470d6ba501d9c4a5d804a. Direct PDF inspection reproduced Figure 5's seven Long-CLIP values, Figure 6's six forced-choice percentages, Table 1's three 3B ablation values, and the visual failure cases. Ten immutable-version primary arXiv competitors were rechecked on 2026-08-23; the pass adds the materially omitted pre-target VectorGym and the later current RefineSVG.
